title: Project Hail Mary Broke a Record Nobody Expected
excerpt: Ryan Gosling's sci-fi opened to $80.5M — Amazon MGM's biggest ever and $15M above projections. Why a hard sci-fi film beat every forecast.
author: StarScoop Daily Staff
imageAlt: Project Hail Mary backdrop — Ryan Gosling sci-fi box office record
metaDescription: Project Hail Mary opened to $80.5M domestic and $140.9M global — Amazon MGM's biggest ever. The numbers, the cast, and why it worked.
content:
Project Hail Mary was projected to open around $65 million. It did $80.5 million.

That is Amazon MGM's biggest opening ever, and it came from a hard science-fiction film about a man solving a physics problem alone in space. Here's why it worked.

DetailInfo
Domestic opening$80.5 million
Global opening$140.9 million
StarringRyan Gosling, Sandra Hüller
DirectorsPhil Lord & Christopher Miller
Scores95% critics · 96% audience · IMDb 8.2

The Numbers

The records it took:

  • Amazon MGM's biggest opening ever — beating Creed III, which did $58 million in 2023
  • Biggest debut of 2026 at the time, passing Scream 7's $63 million
  • $140.9 million globally in its opening weekend

The gap between forecast and result is the interesting part. Tracking had it at roughly $65 million. Beating a projection by $15 million means the audience that showed up was not the audience the models were counting.

It has since been overtaken as the year's biggest opening by The Super Mario Galaxy Movie. But Mario is a sequel to a billion-dollar animated franchise. This is an original-adaptation science-fiction drama.

The budget was around $200 million before marketing, so the opening was necessary rather than merely impressive.

What the Film Actually Is

Adapted from Andy Weir's novel, the premise is deliberately narrow. Science teacher Ryland Grace wakes on a spaceship light years from home with no memory of who he is or how he got there.

As his memory returns he uncovers the mission: solve the riddle of a mysterious substance causing the sun to die out, using scientific knowledge and unorthodox thinking, or everything on Earth ends.

That is a film about a man doing calculations. Weir's The Martian worked the same way, and both live or die on whether the audience finds problem-solving itself dramatic.

Sandra Hüller in the supporting cast is a serious signal — she came out of Anatomy of a Fall and The Zone of Interest, neither of which anyone would call commercial.

Why Lord and Miller Were the Right Choice

The directing credit is the detail that explains the result.

Phil Lord and Christopher Miller made Spider-Man: Into the Spider-Verse, The Lego Movie and 21 Jump Street — films built on premises that sounded unfilmable and worked anyway.

Their actual specialism is tonal control: keeping something funny and sincere at the same time, without either undercutting the other. That is precisely what a story about a lonely scientist saving Earth needs, because played straight it is grim and played light it is weightless.

A 95% critics score with a 96% audience score is the rarest outcome in film. Those numbers usually diverge. When they don't, it means the film delivered on exactly what it promised.

The Honest Caveat

A $200 million budget on an original science-fiction property is a genuinely risky bet, and the opening alone does not clear it.

Films at this budget typically need somewhere around two and a half times production cost to be profitable once marketing and exhibitor splits are counted. A strong opening starts that, it does not finish it.

The scores suggest good word of mouth, which is what actually carries a film of this type — The Martian made most of its money in the weeks after opening rather than during. Reports have pointed to strong holds here too.

What It Signals

Two things worth taking from this.

Original science fiction can still open big. The received wisdom is that only franchises open. An adaptation of a novel with no prior films beat every projection.

Amazon MGM is now a genuine theatrical player. Streaming-owned studios have mostly treated cinemas as a formality before the platform. This was a real theatrical release with a real result.
